card.hook: Picture a whole row of tall, narrow wooden gables squeezed shoulder to shoulder along the harbour, like a crowd posing for a group photo. Your phone is going to love this spot.
card.stand_here: Head to the spot near Bellgården and stand about 30 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face north, and the long line of gabled buildings sits in front of you with the harbour beside it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole row as your eye sees it. If you can't step back far enough, drop to zoom 0.5x to fit it all in, then try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for gables, signs and window details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the vertical edges of the buildings with them so they don't lean, and keep your phone level so the fronts don't look like they're falling backwards.
card.best_time: Late afternoon to evening usually gives warmer light on the fronts. Early morning is typically quieter if you want fewer people in your shot.
card.selfie_here: Walk to the far end of the Bryggen pier, where the open harbour water begins, and face the water so the row of wooden buildings is behind you. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and let the wharf sit over your shoulder (this angle should work, but it's our best guess, so check your screen).
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by near the Hanseatic Museum to take your photo from there, since the higher angle takes in the whole row of buildings.
card.rules_and_safety: Rain makes the cobblestones slippery, so wear good shoes. Check the official site before you go if you want to enter any museum or building.
card.challenge: Play 'spot the details': find a gable top, a door and a window shutter, and get a close-up of each before you leave.
card.good_to_know: Bryggen means 'the dock', and it's also called Tyskebryggen, 'the German dock'. A Hanseatic League Kontor was set up here around 1350, and the wharf has been on the UNESCO World Heritage list since 1979. The buildings you see today are much younger than the site, as the wharf was rebuilt after a big fire in 1702.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the spot near Bellgården and stand about 30 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face north, and the long line of gabled buildings sits in front of you with the harbour beside it.

card.hook: Picture a blue car and a red car sliding past each other on a Bergen hillside, then doing it again a few minutes later. The railway is the star here, and it keeps putting on a show.
card.stand_here: Ride up to the Fjellveien stop, then walk a little back uphill and face the track where the two cars pass. Check the exact spot on the map before you set off.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so you get both cars and the track in one shot. If you can't get far enough back, try 0.5x, and use 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to fill the frame with the pair as they pass.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and run the track along one of the diagonal lines so the climb looks steep and dramatic.
card.best_time: Go in the daytime, when departures run roughly every quarter of an hour, so a missed pair isn't a disaster. Check the Fløibanen timetable before you go.
card.selfie_here: At the Fjellveien stop, spin to the front camera and try to squeeze one of the passing cars in behind you, since it makes a distinctive backdrop. Up at the top station, the left side of the main viewing platform is named as the best angle for a selfie with the view.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by and ask them to stand across Vetrlidsallmenningen, while you stand on the street side in front of the white lower station building so the whole station fits in.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep your distance from the track and stay on the public path. The funicular itself is ticketed, so check the official site before you go; Fjellveien is a public street.
card.challenge: Wait for the blue and red cars to be level with each other, and snap the exact moment they meet.
card.good_to_know: Fløibanen opened on 15 January 1918 and carries nearly two million passengers a year. The line is 848 m long and climbs 302 m, with a passing loop in the middle where the cars meet. The cars are called Blåmann (blue) and Rødhette (red), and with the white lower station they echo the colours of the Norwegian flag.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Ride up to the Fjellveien stop, then walk a little back uphill and face the track where the two cars pass. Check the exact spot on the map before you set off.

card.hook: Eight minutes ago you were in Bergen's streets, and now the whole harbour, the old rooftops and the islands are laid out below you like a model village. Your phone is going to love this one.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, at Mount Fløyen's viewpoint right by the top station of the Fløibanen funicular. Face out over the city and the harbour.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the main view, then go to 0.5x to squeeze in more city and sky. Try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out a boat or a cluster of rooftops.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the top or bottom third line, then tap the city and slide it a little darker if the sky is blown out.
card.best_time: Clear, dry days give you the longest view. Late afternoon or early evening usually brings softer light, and after dark night mode can catch the city lights if you hold your phone very steady.
card.selfie_here: Use the main viewing platform at the top station, where the view drops away over Bergen's rooftops toward the harbour. Switch to the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the city behind you over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: For a shot of you on the platform with the city beyond, ask a passer-by to stand on or beside the bench about a 2-minute walk up the trail from the funicular, while you wave from the platform below.
card.rules_and_safety: Check the Fløibanen operator's official site before you go for current information on the funicular.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole city, then walk up or down a few steps of Fløytrappene and see how much the view changes.
card.good_to_know: Fløyen is one of the seven mountains around Bergen's centre. The viewpoint sits at about 320 m, close to the 400 m top. The Fløibanen opened in 1918, and the viewpoint was rebuilt and extended in 2002 as the broad staircase called Fløytrappene.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, at Mount Fløyen's viewpoint right by the top station of the Fløibanen funicular. Face out over the city and the harbour.

card.hook: A medieval royal hall, a 1560s tower and a Second World War concrete bunker all share one set of walls here, and your phone gets to capture the lot. Bergenhus is the kind of place where one short walk gives you five different pictures.
card.stand_here: Start near Bradbenken: stand about 120 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west. That gives you the big overall view before you walk in closer.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x for the main view of the buildings, then zoom 0.5x for the open grounds and walls. Try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for stonework and rooflines.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the stone wall, then slide the brightness down a touch if the sky looks washed out, so the sky keeps its colour and the buildings don't turn into dark shapes.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is kinder to old stone than midday sun. A cloudy day works nicely too, because the colours stay even and there are no harsh shadows.
card.selfie_here: Walk to the far end of the open grounds. A local tip says the view back towards Bryggen is best from there, and it's quieter than the wharf. Use the front camera, switch to zoom 0.5x, and keep the fortress behind you over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is permitted for personal use throughout the fortress, including inside King Håkon's Hall and Rosenkrantz Tower, but no flash during concerts or events in the hall. The fortress is still under the Royal Norwegian Navy, so check the official site for access and visiting arrangements. The top tower platform has a low protective wall, so take care up there on windy days.
card.challenge: Find a frame where the pale medieval stone and a later addition sit side by side, then add one tiny person for scale.
card.good_to_know: Bergenhus is one of the oldest and best preserved stone fortifications in Norway. The area, then called Holmen, was the royal seat of Bergen, and Bergen was Norway's capital in the 13th century until 1299. Haakon's Hall dates from around 1260, and about 150 military personnel are still stationed here today.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start near Bradbenken: stand about 120 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west. That gives you the big overall view before you walk in closer.

card.hook: Trays of seafood, handwritten signs and a trolley rolling past your elbow: Bergen Fish Market is busy, and that's exactly why it photographs so well. Every few steps there's a new little story.
card.stand_here: Head for Bergen Fish Market, near Strandkaien, and stand about 15 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face south-east.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the main view of the market. If the stalls are crowded and you can't step back, try 0.5x. Then use 2x or higher (depends on your phone) for close-ups of food and signs.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest or most colourful stall, then drag the brightness down a touch so bright signs and white ice trays don't wash out.
card.best_time: Go when the market is open but not too crowded, so you can see the stalls clearly. Soft morning or late-afternoon light is kinder on colours than harsh midday sun. Check the official site for trading times before you go.
card.selfie_here: Flip to the front camera and try zoom 0.5x so more of the colourful stalls fit in. Keep them over your shoulder and hold the phone a little higher than your face.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot from the Torget side facing the stalls, with Bryggen in the background, while you stand between them and the stalls.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a working market, so be ready to step aside for customers and trolleys. Ask before photographing people, and avoid pointing your phone at faces from very close.
card.challenge: Find a repeating pattern, like a row of awnings or a line of people, and make it the star of one photo.
card.good_to_know: Bergen Fish Market is a lively working market for food and shopping, with plenty happening at close range. Start wide to show the whole scene, then move in for details. Take a few frames at different heights, one at chest level and one lower, then pick your favourite later.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for Bergen Fish Market, near Strandkaien, and stand about 15 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face south-east.

card.hook: Most people snap Vågen and walk on, but this little bay is where Bergen began, on its eastern shore, before the town spread round the south and west. So your water photo is also a photo of the old town's first days.
card.stand_here: Head to Østre Murallmenningen and stand about 460 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face north-west and the harbour is right in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the water and the buildings on the far shore. Tap 0.5x to squeeze more of the bay into one frame, then try 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out the old buildings across the water.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and put the far shoreline on the lower or upper third line, so it doesn't slice the picture in half.
card.best_time: Early morning or the hour before sunset gives softer light and calmer water. After dark, switch on night mode and rest your elbows on something solid so the shot stays sharp.
card.selfie_here: Try the Bergenhus Fortress grounds, beside Rosenkrantz Tower, with the harbour open behind you. Use the front camera, tap 0.5x if you can, and hold the phone a little higher so the water fills the background.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the waterfront across the harbour from Bryggen while you stand in front of the water, so the harbour and quayside fill the background.
card.rules_and_safety: The bay is a central part of the city, but some harbour-side and waterfront sites may have their own access rules, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take three frames in three minutes: one wide for the whole bay, one tighter on the far shore, and one with a boat or the water's edge in the foreground.
card.good_to_know: Vågen is the central harbour of Bergen, about 1,200 metres long, and it opens out from the larger Byfjorden. Bergenhus Fortress and Bryggen sit on the northern shore, and the Nordnes peninsula lies along the south. Bryggen is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and some of its old buildings date back to the 11th century.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to Østre Murallmenningen and stand about 460 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face north-west and the harbour is right in front of you.

card.hook: Seals and penguins have zero interest in your photo plans, and they move fast. Good news: the outdoor ponds are the easiest place to start, because the animals are out in open daylight.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map. It sits in the middle of the aquarium site on the Nordnes peninsula, so there's no extra walking once you arrive. Face the outdoor ponds, with the aquarium buildings as a plain, solid backdrop.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x for the buildings and the layout of the outdoor area, and 1x for the ponds and most tanks. Try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for seals and penguins across the water, but only in bright outdoor light. Indoors it can look grainy.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the animal, then drag the slider to make the picture a little darker if the water or sky is washing out.
card.best_time: Pick a bright but overcast day, or go in the morning, when the light is soft and even for the outdoor ponds. Indoor tanks look much the same at any hour, so just choose a quieter moment if you want clear space at the glass.
card.selfie_here: Try Nordnes Park (Nordnesparken), the park behind the aquarium building. It's described as having views over the fjord and mountains. No exact standing spot is known, so wander a little and check the angle on the spot. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x to fit more in, and hold the phone slightly high with the scenery over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across from the hop-on-hop-off bus stop No. 5, directly in front of the aquarium entrance on Nordnesbakken, while you stand by the stop so the building is behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally allowed inside, but skip the flash because it can disturb the animals.
card.challenge: Get down to penguin eye level and snap a few frames, leaving a little space in front of the way it's heading. Then pick your favourite.
card.good_to_know: Bergen Aquarium opened on 27 August 1960, when it was considered the largest and most modern aquarium in Northern Europe. The buildings were designed in 1952 by architects Hans Chr. Gaaserud and Helge Simers, and a cinema was added in 1995. Inside you'll find more than 300 species and over 60 tanks.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map. It sits in the middle of the aquarium site on the Nordnes peninsula, so there's no extra walking once you arrive. Face the outdoor ponds, with the aquarium buildings as a plain, solid backdrop.

card.hook: Forget the postcard for a minute: the star here is the wood itself, with its uneven walls, narrow gables and weathered doors that look best up close.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, which is right at the Hanseatic Museum and Schøtstuene in Finnegården on Bryggen. Face the building front, and take your wide shot from the furthest spot you can comfortably stand.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the frontage as you see it, and try 0.5x if the street is too tight to fit the whole gable. Then step in and use zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for timber joints, windows and signs.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and keep the vertical lines of the wooden walls straight, because tilting your phone up makes the building lean.
card.best_time: Earlier or later in the day usually gives softer light on the wood and fewer people in your shot. Overcast days are fine too, since they show off the texture of the walls.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold it a bit low so the wooden front sits over your shoulder. Check that the gable isn't cut off before you tap the button.
card.ask_someone: Stand on Zachariasbryggen, the quay on Bryggen, and ask a passer-by to frame the whole museum front behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Rain makes the Bryggen cobblestones slippery, so wear good shoes. Photography rules inside may apply (flash is usually banned inside Schøtstuene), so check the official site before you go, including whether the main building is open.
card.challenge: Find a doorway or window and frame it as a little picture inside your picture, with a bit of the neighbouring buildings in view.
card.good_to_know: German merchants had an overseas office at Bryggen by 1360, and for about four centuries the site held their assembly halls. The present building went up after the fire of 1702. Schøtstuene was where the cooking was done, because fire was forbidden in the other Bryggen buildings, which makes a nice caption.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, which is right at the Hanseatic Museum and Schøtstuene in Finnegården on Bryggen. Face the building front, and take your wide shot from the furthest spot you can comfortably stand.

ask_someone_spot.detail: Stand on Zachariasbryggen and ask the visitor to pose with the museum in view. card.hook: Plain stone walls, one clear shape and a big sky behind it: Rosenkrantz Tower is about as easy to photograph as a building gets. Even a quick snap looks good.
card.stand_here: Start near Festningskaien, at the phone icon on the map, about 120 m south of the subject. Face north and take your first shot from there.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole tower. If you walk close and it won't fit, drop to zoom 0.5x. For stonework and the roofline, try zoom 2x or 5x if your phone has them.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the stone wall, then slide the brightness down a touch if the sky looks too bright, so the sky keeps its colour and the stone keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, warmer light on the stone. Either is a nice time for a slow stroll around the fortress.
card.selfie_here: Try the main gate of Bergenhus Fortress, on the approach from Bryggen wharf, since that's the way into the tower. Use the front camera at 0.5x and angle yourself so the tower sits over your shoulder. Nobody has confirmed an exact selfie spot, so wiggle around until it fits.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the fortress gateway on the Bryggen side with the tower in view and to shoot from a low angle, while you stand in front of the tower.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are allowed inside the tower, but flash isn't always allowed and some exhibit areas may have limits. The tower has many tiny steps and narrow stairways, so it may not suit visitors with mobility issues. Access can change, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get one full-length shot of the tower, then one close-up of a window or the roofline, and see which one your friends like more.
card.good_to_know: The oldest part is a medieval tower from the 1270s, built under King Magnus the Lawmender. It was altered around 1520, then enlarged and reshaped in the 1560s by Scottish stonemasons and architects. The name comes from Erik Rosenkrantz, governor of the fortress from 1560 to 1568. Haakon's Hall is in the same fortress, so you can add it to your walk.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start near Festningskaien, at the phone icon on the map, about 120 m south of the subject. Face north and take your first shot from there.

card.hook: The oldest building in Bergen still standing has two chunky grey towers, and they fit in your phone screen like they were designed for it. Okay, they were built about 850 years before phones, but the simple outline helps.
card.stand_here: Stand on Dreggsallmenningen, at the Bryggen end of the street, and face south toward the church. You want the facade and both towers, with the Snorre monument and the Bryggens Museum building alongside.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the facade, both towers and the Snorre monument in one go. If the street feels too narrow, tap 0.5x, but keep the church away from the edges so it doesn't look stretched. Try 2x or more (depends on your phone) for a tighter shot of the towers.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and keep your phone upright, so the towers stand straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Early morning or an overcast day should give soft, even light on the grey stone. You should also get fewer people in front of the monument.
card.selfie_here: Head into the churchyard in front of Mariakirken and turn so the facade is behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a little low and wide (try 0.5x if your phone has it), and let the towers rise over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the western approach, while you stand in front of the twin-tower facade, so the whole church fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is not allowed inside the church, so keep to exterior shots. It's a place of worship and is closed to sightseeing at weekends outside services, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the Snorre monument low in the frame with both towers rising behind it, and no stranger's head sneaking into the shot.
card.good_to_know: Building probably began in the 1130s or 1140s and finished around 1180. It's mainly Romanesque and built largely of soapstone. In 1408 the city's large German population took the church over, and it was popularly called the German church.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Dreggsallmenningen, at the Bryggen end of the street, and face south toward the church. You want the facade and both towers, with the Snorre monument and the Bryggens Museum building alongside.

selfie_spots.why: <cite index="11-10">The churchyard can be walked around at any time</cite>, so you can use it outdoors even when the interior is closed.

card.hook: There's a cannonball stuck in the wall of this church, and it's been there since the 1665 Battle of Vågen. Most people walk right past it while they're busy photographing the tower.
card.stand_here: Stand on Domkirkeplassen, the square in front of the west façade, and face the church tower. The cathedral lies to the east, about 1 minute on foot to the middle of the building.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the façade and tower together, because it keeps the building looking natural. If the square is crowded and you can't step back, try 0.5x. Use 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the top of the tower and the cannonball.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, hold your phone upright and level, and put the tower on one of the vertical lines with a little sky above it.
card.best_time: Daytime is best for a clear shot of the outside of the cathedral.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and try 0.5x so you and the landmark both fit, with the building over your shoulder. Hold the phone a little higher than your face and take a few, because the first one is never the keeper.
card.rules_and_safety: People may be coming and going at the door, so keep the doorway clear while you shoot. Check opening and service times before you plan to go inside.
card.challenge: Find the cannonball in the wall, take a close-up, and use the 1665 story as your caption.
card.good_to_know: The cathedral is dedicated to Saint Olaf, and the first written mention of a church on this site is from 1181. It has burned and been rebuilt several times. After the fires of 1623 and 1640 it took on the look you see today, square west tower included.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Domkirkeplassen, the square in front of the west façade, and face the church tower. The cathedral lies to the east, about 1 minute on foot to the middle of the building.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found describes a spot where a visitor can stand with the cathedral behind them, so I have no selfie spot to recommend. The sources mention the cathedral's exterior and surrounding streets in general terms, and one describes a cannonball lodged in the western wall, but none says where to stand for a selfie. Interior photos are reportedly allowed for personal use, but no page gives a selfie-stick or tripod rule. For a passer-by position, the cathedral's address is Domkirkeplassen 1, 5003 Bergen, but no page says where to stand to frame the whole building, so I did not name one. A visitor could check the square at Domkirkeplassen on a map and test angles there.

card.hook: Grieg Hall is about 184 m wide, so your phone's first instinct is to make it look tiny. Here's how to win that argument.
card.stand_here: Head for the spot near Nygårdsgaten and stand at the phone icon, about 25 m west of the building. Face east and you'll have room for plenty of the frontage.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze the whole hall in, then switch to 1x for a more natural look. For a close-up of the facade, try zoom 2x or 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the roof and the base of the building with them, so the long horizontal lines stay straight instead of sloping.
card.best_time: Soft daylight in the morning or late afternoon suits big buildings best. On a bright day, watch for glare, and after dark try night mode if the building is lit.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x, hold your arm out and turn so the long building sits behind your shoulder. Take a few, because wide shots are forgiving and you'll want one where nobody walks through.
card.rules_and_safety: The official Grieghallen page says photography is allowed only where explicitly stated, never with flash, and phones should be switched off during performances.
card.challenge: Take three shots of the same wall: all of it, then a section, then just a pattern of lines and reflections. Which one would you frame?
card.good_to_know: Grieg Hall (Grieghallen) is a 1,500-seat concert hall named after Bergen-born composer Edvard Grieg, and the Bergen Philharmonic Orchestra still calls it home. Danish architect Knud Munk designed it in a modernist style, with building starting in 1967 and finishing by May 1978. It also hosted the Eurovision Song Contest in 1986.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the spot near Nygårdsgaten and stand at the phone icon, about 25 m west of the building. Face east and you'll have room for plenty of the frontage.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a specific selfie spot or a passer-by photo position with Grieghallen behind or in frame, so I have left both empty rather than guess. Shothotspot (https://shothotspot.com/hotspots/?acc=&country=&kw=&nelat=60.5268&nelng=5.6878&place=Bergen%2C+Norway&swlat=60.2035&swlng=5.1706&types=) lists 'Grieg Hall' as a photo location but gives no vantage point. Wikimedia Commons has a 'Lille Lungegårdsvannet' category that includes Grieghallen in its captions, but no page names a viewpoint on the lake or its shore. Bergen guides (visitBergen PDF, https://www.visitbergen.com/dbimgs/Bergen-Guide-en-2025.pdf) recommend the harbour side of Bryggen, not Grieghallen. The official Grieghallen page (https://www.fib.no/en/practical-information/venues/grieghallen) states photography is allowed only where explicitly stated, never with flash, and that phones should be switched off during performances; it says nothing about selfie sticks or tripods. No page I found states selfie-stick or tripod rules for this venue, and none mentions a safety point. A local check of the lake shore or Edvard Griegs plass is advisable before publishing any spot.

card.hook: Torgallmenningen is about 218 m across, which is a lot of square, so don't squeeze it into one tight shot. Think wide, think everyday Bergen, with the Sjømannsmonumentet standing tall in the middle.
card.stand_here: You're near Torgallmenningen. Stand about 20 m north-west of the subject, right at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. The monument is about 20 m away in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x to get the full width of the square, then switch to 1x for the monument. Try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pull the monument closer without walking up to it.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines, put the monument on a vertical line, and check the corners so the buildings at the edges stay straight.
card.best_time: Pick a quieter time if you can, so you get fewer people in the frame. Soft daylight is kinder to the monument than harsh midday sun.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the Sailors' Monument (Sjømannsmonumentet) in the middle of Torgallmenningen, so the open square and the buildings are behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more of the scene in, and keep the monument close to you.
card.challenge: Take the monument twice: first a sideways wide shot with a few walkers in it to show the scale, then an upright one that fills the frame.
card.good_to_know: Torgallmenningen is the main square of Bergen. Its name means roughly 'general public square', and it was once spelled Torvalmenningen. The Sjømannsmonumentet is its best-known feature.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: You're near Torgallmenningen. Stand about 20 m north-west of the subject, right at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. The monument is about 20 m away in front of you.

card.hook: Here's a Bergen surprise: the best photo of Nordnes isn't taken on Nordnes. You head up the mountain and look back down at it, which is why guides call it the postcard view.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Fløyen summit viewpoint, on the terrace above the city, and face down over the peninsula toward the fjord. Nordnes runs diagonally across the right side of the view, with Lille Lungegårdsvannet on the left.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x or 1x to get the whole city panorama in. Then tap 2x or 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the peninsula for a second, tighter shot.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, put the fjord horizon on a lower line, and let the peninsula run from the middle of the frame toward the right-hand edge.
card.best_time: Two guides recommend sunrise and late afternoon. Aim for one of those and the harbour and mountains will do half the work for you.
card.selfie_here: Head out to the viewing platform at Nordnesparken, at the tip of the peninsula. Use the front camera at 0.5x, with the trees and shoreline behind you and the harbour view opening out beyond. For a more colourful backdrop, try the narrow wooden-house lanes west of Klosteret, which one guide calls the most photographed lanes in the area.
card.ask_someone: On the main viewing platform at the top of Fløyen, near the grandstand area, ask a passer-by to shoot down toward the city with the peninsula angled on the right of the frame, while you stand in the foreground.
card.rules_and_safety: Fløyen is reached by a paid funicular (a hiking route also gets you there), so check the official site before you go. The path to Nordnesparken can be steep, and in the lived-in lanes, be mindful of residents' privacy.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot and one zoomed shot from the same spot, then see which one your friends like better.
card.good_to_know: Nordnes is the long finger of land pushing into the water right beside Bergen's city centre, with Vågen, Byfjorden and Puddefjorden around it. The Bergen Aquarium sits at its tip. Fredriksberg Fortress, the Norwegian Institute of Marine Research and the parish church, Nykirken, are on the peninsula too.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the Fløyen summit viewpoint, on the terrace above the city, and face down over the peninsula toward the fjord. Nordnes runs diagonally across the right side of the view, with Lille Lungegårdsvannet on the left.

card.hook: Most lakes are blobs. This one in the middle of Bergen is a neat octagon with a big fountain in the centre, like someone drew it with a ruler. Your phone will love it.
card.stand_here: Stand on Rasmus Meyers allé, about 35 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face north-east and the fountain is right in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the lake and fountain together. Tap 0.5x to squeeze in more of the octagon and the park, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the fountain.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the fountain, then slide the brightness down a touch if the sky is bright, so the spray stays white and sparkly instead of blown out.
card.best_time: Early morning or a still, overcast day usually gives the calmest water and the best reflections. Late afternoon gives softer light across the park, and spring is lovely when the trees blossom.
card.selfie_here: Turn on the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and stand with the lake and fountain over your shoulder. Hold the phone a little higher than your face so you fit more of the scene in.
card.ask_someone: Try asking a passer-by at Festplassen, the square beside the lake, to take your photo while you stand a few steps towards the water with the lake behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Check the official site before you go for any local restrictions or work in the park.
card.challenge: Get two shots: one standing, then one crouched low near the water to see how much bigger the reflections get.
card.good_to_know: Lille Lungegårdsvannet, also called Smålungeren, is about 279 m across and used to be much larger. The edges were filled in as the city grew until the octagon took its present shape in the mid-20th century. A strait once joined it to Store Lungegårdsvannet, but that was filled in in 1926 and replaced by an underground culvert, so the lake still rises and falls a little with the tide.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Rasmus Meyers allé, about 35 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face north-east and the fountain is right in front of you.

No selfie stick or tripod rules and no safety points were found on these pages.

card.hook: From down the street, KODE looks small, almost modest for a group of art museums. That's your first decision: do you want the building, or the whole street with people walking through?
card.stand_here: Stand on Rasmus Meyers allé, about 290 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face south-east.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the whole scene. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to bring the museum closer without walking any nearer. Use 0.5x only if you step in close and want the whole frontage in.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and line the building up with one of the vertical lines so it doesn't look like it's leaning.
card.best_time: Soft light on an overcast day, or in the morning, gives the building nice even colours. Bergen's weather changes fast, so check the sky first. Wet pavements can add a pretty reflection, and in the evening night mode helps if the light fades (hold still while it works).
card.selfie_here: Walk the path or sit on a bench around Lille Lungegårdsvann, the lake, with the KODE buildings behind you. Use the front camera, and if it has a 0.5x button, try it so more of the museums fit over your shoulder. The exact spot is approximate, so wander until the building shows behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: If you want photos inside the galleries, the rules on photography can differ from room to room, so check the official KODE website before you go.
card.challenge: Take two shots from the same spot: one wide with the street and people, one zoomed on just the museum. Which one would you put on the fridge?
card.good_to_know: KODE is Bergen's group of art museums, and these buildings are in the city centre. This makes a tidy photo to remember the visit by, especially if you're going inside afterwards. Check the official KODE website for visiting information before you go.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Rasmus Meyers allé, about 290 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face south-east.

card.hook: Picture a stone hall that has survived fires, raids and a spell as a storage shed, and still looks this calm. That's Haakon's Hall, and its plain walls and steep lines are made for a photo taken from a little way back.
card.stand_here: Stand about 25 m south-west of the hall, near Festningskaien, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. Walk towards the middle of the fortress grounds until the whole hall fits in your frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole hall. If you're close to the walls and can't step back, try zoom 0.5x, then zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the stonework, windows and roofline.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the hall's vertical edges with them, keeping your phone upright so the walls stay straight.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light on the stone and fewer people in the grounds. On an overcast day the walls look even, so you can shoot any time.
card.selfie_here: Head onto the open grounds of Bergenhus Fortress and stand where Vågen harbour is in front of you and the hall is behind you. Switch to the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and the hall will sit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the side of the hall that faces Vågen, which is the best side to photograph it from, while you stand a few steps back from the wall so the whole building fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are fine in the fortress area, and inside the hall when there's no concert, but photography isn't allowed during performances. Entry rules and times can change, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot with a bit of lawn in the foreground, then one close-up of the stonework, and see if a friend can guess they're the same building.
card.good_to_know: Haakon's Hall was built in the middle of the 13th century in the reign of King Håkon Håkonsson, and it's the largest secular medieval building in Norway. It was badly damaged by fire on 20 April 1944, then reopened on 11 September 1961, exactly 700 years after its first recorded use. Today it hosts occasional concerts and official banquets.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 25 m south-west of the hall, near Festningskaien, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. Walk towards the middle of the fortress grounds until the whole hall fits in your frame.

selfie_research.notes: Only one selfie spot was supported by a page; the Vågen-facing side is the strongest page-backed photo position, but no page gives a precise point on the grounds, so the selfie spot is approximate. The gofjords guide is about three years old. A Flickr caption names a vantage 'just north of the Håkon Håkonssons ringmur' (girdle wall) in Bergenhus Fortress, which could serve as an alternative photo position, but it is a caption, not a guide. A concert page says photography is not permitted during performances at Håkonshallen, though photos are allowed in the fortress area and in the hall when there is no concert. No page gives selfie-stick or tripod rules. A guide's remark about not having to climb the fortress walls is not stated as a safety point, so I left the safety field empty.

card.hook: Some buildings just look like they're standing up straight on purpose. Permanenten is one of them, with a formal, symmetrical façade that makes a tilted phone look like a crime.
card.stand_here: Stand on Nordahl Bruns gate, about 15 m north-west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map. Face south-east and step back if you want more of the building in.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural view of the façade. If you're too close to fit it all in, tap 0.5x and keep the phone upright. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for windows, stonework and the entrance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the walls with the vertical lines so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon gives soft light that's kind to the façade. An overcast day works too, with even light and fewer harsh shadows.
card.selfie_here: Head to Byparken, the park beside Permanenten, and put the building behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the façade over your shoulder. A reviewer says the summer flowers make for nice pictures.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the pavement in front of the main entrance, so they can fit the building and the large sculpture above the door behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are allowed for private use without flash, and the museum asks you to keep your phone handheld. No photos or video during concerts, and commercial photos need the museum's approval. Check the museum's official info before you go if you want to shoot inside.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot and one tight shot of the same façade, then see which one you'd actually put on the fridge.
card.good_to_know: The museum began in 1887 as an idea of Johan Bøgh, and in 1896 it moved into this building, designed by Henry Bucher. It caught fire during the 1916 Bergen Fire but was saved. Inside you'll find crafts from the past 500 years, like silver, furniture, glass, porcelain and textiles, plus a well-known Chinese collection.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Nordahl Bruns gate, about 15 m north-west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map. Face south-east and step back if you want more of the building in.

selfie_research.notes: Naming conflict: the brief says Permanenten is KODE 4, but several sources say Permanenten is KODE 1 and that KODE 4 is now Lysverket on Rasmus Meyers allé 9 (lifeinnorway.net). The coordinates you gave match Permanenten's listed location (Wikidata: 60°23'28"N, 5°19'26"E), so I treated the landmark as Permanenten. Only one selfie spot is backed by a page: the sources name Byparken but do not describe an exact camera position, so 'in the park with the building behind you' is a general placement. The entrance-pavement spot for the passer-by is also unconfirmed as a framing position for the whole building. Sources are mixed on age: the KODE Permanenten page mentions renovation and limited exhibitions in 2022–23, so check current status. No page found gives a tripod or selfie-stick rule for this site, and no safety point was found.
